title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Overview
Satellite cropland maps differ in how much cropland they show and in what they count as cropland. In North Africa, independent field-based reference data to evaluate them are scarce. This project builds a field-based reference for the principal cereal-producing regions of Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia and uses it to estimate cropland area and to assess satellite cropland products.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Approach
A probability-based field survey across all three countries, with 1,350 field observations collected during the 2023–2024 season. Design-based estimators provide cropland area estimates with quantified uncertainty, and the same reference sample supports an independent accuracy assessment of publicly available satellite cropland products.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Research contributions

A probability-sampled, field-based reference dataset for dryland cereal systems in a region where such data are scarce.
An independent evaluation of how publicly available satellite cropland products represent North African dryland agriculture.

Quantitative results will appear in a manuscript currently in preparation.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance in North Africa
text:
Overview
Drought monitoring records physical anomalies, but not the moment environmental stress becomes publicly recognized and institutionally actionable. Across North Africa, governments periodically organize Islamic rain rituals (Ṣalāt al-Istisqāʾ) in response to water scarcity, and their official announcements leave a dated, public record of that moment. This project treats state-organized rain rituals as observable institutional responses to drought, distinct from the physical conditions that precede them.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance in North Africa
text:
Approach
A 25-year archival record of 63 state-organized rain rituals in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia (2000–2024), linked to drought indicators computed over cropland.



Archival research for the rain-ritual record.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance in North Africa
text:
Research contributions

Introduces state-organized rain rituals as a dated, publicly recorded signal of when drought becomes institutionally recognized.
Institutional recognition of drought follows agricultural drought: it concentrates in the rainfed cropping season and in the main rainfed regions.
Rain rituals mark when stress becomes publicly visible; they do not measure drought or its impacts.

Full results appear in the forthcoming article.






In the news. When a Prayer Is Also a Climate Signal. Eos (AGU), 3 December 2025.

title: Drought and Long-Term Agricultural Land-Use Change in North Africa
text:
Overview
Most climate–agriculture research focuses on crop yield or production. Drought can also change whether land is planted, kept in cultivation, left fallow or withdrawn from cropping, and these effects on the extent of cultivation remain poorly documented. This project examines long-term cropland expansion and contraction across Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia and its relationship with drought.

title: Drought and Long-Term Agricultural Land-Use Change in North Africa
text:
Approach
Long-term satellite cropland records (2000–2024) combined with gridded drought indicators and statistical modeling of cropland expansion and contraction.

title: Drought and Long-Term Agricultural Land-Use Change in North Africa
text:
Research contributions
The analysis addresses an under-studied pathway of drought impact: change in the extent of cultivated land, rather than in yield or production. Results will appear in a manuscript currently in preparation.

title: Doctoral research
text:
I completed my PhD in Geographical Sciences at the University of Maryland in 2026, directed by Tatiana V. Loboda and mentored by Molly E. Brown. My dissertation, Drought and Agricultural Land-Use Change in North Africa, examined how drought shapes agricultural land use across Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia.
From the start, I wanted to put people in the equation. Satellites show where farmland changes, but not how societies experience drought. So alongside satellite and climate records, I read drought through the moment states publicly recognize it: state-organized rain rituals.
The work also meant going to the fields. Over the 2023–2024 season I drove thousands of kilometres through the cereal belt of all three countries, collecting independent field observations of the region’s farmland.

title: About
text:
Walid Ouaret is an Earth observation scientist and a Postdoctoral Fellow at The Earth Commons Institute, Georgetown University, where he works with Roshanak (Roshi) Nateghi in the SuRGE Lab. His research examines how climate extremes affect agricultural landscapes, critical infrastructure and the institutions that manage environmental risk.
He received his Ph.D. in Geographical Sciences from the University of Maryland, College Park in 2026. His dissertation, Drought and Agricultural Land-Use Change in North Africa, was directed by Tatiana V. Loboda, with mentorship from Molly E. Brown. It combined fieldwork across Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia with satellite, climate and archival records.
Before his doctorate, he worked on landscape and agricultural modeling at INRAE (Montpellier and Paris) and at Wageningen University, and on remote sensing and GIS research at Miami University’s Geospatial Analysis Center. He trained as an agronomist at the École Nationale Supérieure Agronomique in Algiers. He holds master’s degrees from Paris-Saclay University and AgroParisTech, and from the Mediterranean Agronomic Institute of Chania. He co-developed the NASA-funded Open Climate Science for Agriculture curriculum, taught in English, French and Arabic.

title: Agricultural and Environmental Modeling
section: Crop allocation in Tunisian rainfed smallholder systems
text:
Crop allocation in Tunisian rainfed smallholder systems
INRAE Landscape Modeling Team, Montpellier · 2018–2020 · IRD-ARTS grant (PI: Jean-Stéphane Bailly, AgroParisTech)
I collected data through farmer interviews and seasonal crop monitoring in the Lebna watershed using remote sensing. I combined these with expert elicitation to build and validate a crop allocation model for Tunisia’s rainfed smallholder farming systems.

title: Agricultural and Environmental Modeling

Liming trade-offs in western Kenya
Plant Production Systems Group, Wageningen University · 2018
I built a database of field experiments on lime use in maize across Sub-Saharan Africa and ran a trade-off analysis linking yield effects to greenhouse gas emissions and farm income.

title: Agricultural Greenhouse Mapping in Algeria
text:
Overview
Satellite imagery and deep learning are used to characterize the spatial distribution of greenhouse agriculture in Algeria and support the monitoring of intensive agricultural land use. The research develops an Earth observation approach for identifying greenhouse structures across agricultural landscapes.
Greenhouse agriculture is a form of intensification that is spreading quickly in Algeria, especially in the southern wilayas, and it is poorly documented in agricultural statistics and land-cover products.

title: Agricultural Greenhouse Mapping in Algeria
text:
Approach
Deep learning applied to satellite imagery to detect greenhouse structures across Algerian agricultural landscapes.



Greenhouse area in the leading wilayas, 2000 and 2021.

title: Agricultural Greenhouse Mapping in Algeria
text:
Research contributions
An Earth observation approach to mapping greenhouse structures where agricultural statistics and land-cover products document them poorly, published at IEEE M2GARSS 2024. The mapping work is ongoing.

title: Research
text:
Cereal fields, Bizerte region, northern Tunisia · fieldwork, May 2024
The research program links satellite Earth observation, field surveys, climate records and archival data to document how climate extremes reshape agricultural land use and how societies and institutions respond. Fieldwork has centred on the drylands of Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia; current work at Georgetown extends the program to climate risks for critical infrastructure.

title: Research
text:
01 · Earth Observation & Agricultural Change

Established
Satellite remote sensing, cropland mapping, agricultural monitoring, probability-based field surveys and land-use dynamics in dryland environments. This work builds field reference datasets, assesses satellite cropland products, and relates drought to cropland extent and agricultural intensification across Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia.



Completed · manuscript in preparation

Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation
A probability-based field survey, design-based area estimation and an independent assessment of satellite cropland maps.




Completed · manuscript in preparation

Drought and Long-Term Agricultural Land-Use Change
Long-term cropland change across the region (2000–2024) and its relationship with drought.




In progress

NASA HarvestStat
Subnational crop production statistics for North Africa, and the evolution, volatility and climate sensitivity of wheat systems.




Published · ongoing

Agricultural Greenhouse Mapping in Algeria
Deep learning on satellite imagery to map greenhouse structures and monitor intensive agricultural land use (IEEE M2GARSS 2024).

title: Research
text:
02 · Climate Signals & Societal Response

Established
Drought indicators, institutional recognition of environmental stress, climate governance and observable societal responses to climate extremes. This work studies institutional responses to drought, the role of environmental information in decision-making and climate-risk communication. State-organized rain rituals are treated as observable institutional responses, distinct from the physical drought conditions that precede them.





Accepted · Environmental Research: Climate

Rain Rituals and Drought Governance in North Africa
A 25-year archival record of 63 state-organized rain rituals in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia, linked to drought indicators over cropland. Featured in Eos (AGU), 2025.

title: SEEDS: Satellite-Enabled Earth Observation & Digital Solutions for Agriculture
text:
Role: Project Lead · Funding: 6th Grain · Period: 2025–2026
SEEDS puts satellite Earth observation and digital tools to work for agricultural decision-making. From October 14 to 17, 2025, the project ran the SEEDS Seminar Series: four days of talks on remote sensing and AI for agriculture and food security. It was held online and hosted by the Department of Geographical Sciences, University of Maryland. Speakers came from NASA Harvest, NASA Acres, Harvard and the University of Montana.
